source: Original KaiSip study notes, organized by The IIA's CIA Part 1 syllabus effective 2025. KaiSip is an independent study aid, not affiliated with or endorsed by The IIA.
overview: Section D is about fraud: what it is, why people commit it, where it is likely, which controls prevent or detect it, and what an internal auditor does on meeting a sign of it. The Global Internal Audit Standards say little about fraud, but say it firmly: consider fraud risk in every engagement (a single audit assignment), weigh it as part of due professional care, and report concerns through the proper channel. Each standard has requirements, which say 'must', and considerations, which say 'should' or 'may'; these notes mark which is which, because an answer that turns a 'should' into a 'must' overstates the rule. Management owns fraud prevention, and an investigation needs the right mandate and skills.
analogy: Think of a lifeguard at a public pool. The lifeguard does not own the pool, mend the fence or write the rules; the pool manager does. But on every shift the lifeguard scans the water, knowing where swimmers get into trouble: the deep end, the crowded slide, the corner nobody watches. On seeing a sign of trouble, the lifeguard does not wait for the end-of-day report or start a private inquiry, but raises the alarm through the agreed signal. A rescue diver handles what needs diving skills. Internal auditors treat fraud risk in the same way.

topics.topic_name: Fraud triangle, fraud risks and schemes
topics.overview: Fraud is deliberate deception for a gain the person or organization has no right to. This topic explains what sets fraud apart from error, the three sides of the fraud triangle, how to recognize where fraud could happen, and the main families of fraud schemes.
can_do: Explain what separates fraud from an honest error
Describe each side of the fraud triangle and give an example of it
Recognize the conditions that make fraud more likely in a process
Match a described scheme to its family: fraudulent reporting, asset misappropriation or corruption

subtopics.name: Fraud and How It Differs from Error
subtopics.definition: Fraud is a deliberate act of deception, concealment or breach of trust by a person or organization to gain an advantage it is not entitled to.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Intent changes the response. An error needs a process fix; a suspected fraud needs careful reporting, protected evidence and often specialists.
how_it_works: Intent is the dividing line: an error is an honest mistake, while fraud is done on purpose and is usually hidden.
The gain can be money, property, a bonus or a business advantage, and staff, managers, executives, suppliers, customers or outsiders can all commit fraud.
Three clues point toward intent: a pattern instead of a single slip, effort to hide the item, and reluctance to correct it once raised.
Small amounts still count: a practitioner quoted in a 2026 white paper The IIA published with the Anti-Fraud Collaboration warns that frauds tend to start small and grow.
An internal auditor reports what the evidence shows and that it may indicate fraud. Deciding that fraud happened is for an investigation by qualified people.
subtopics.example: At a furniture exporter in Vietnam, junior internal auditor Linh notices five invoices split to stay under an approval limit, with altered dates. The total is small, so Linh files it as a clerical error. A year later the pattern has cost forty times as much. Linh now treats a pattern with concealment as a fraud indicator at any amount and raises it at once.

review: Sample corrected errors for repeats, concealment or resistance to correction
Compare how similar misstatements were classified across units
evidence: Error and adjustment logs with the reason given for each
Records of matters referred for investigation and their outcomes
audit_focus.recommend: Ask management to define when a repeated or concealed error must be referred for investigation.
audit_focus.decides: Qualified investigators establish the facts; management acts on the result

subtopics.isaca_rule: Fraud needs intent; error does not. Must: report a concern through the channel that policy and law set. Sound practice: treat pattern and concealment as indicators of intent, and leave the finding of fraud to an investigation.

exam_traps.trap: The amount is too small to be fraud.
exam_traps.why: Size is not the test. A deliberate, concealed act for gain is fraud at any amount.

exam_traps.trap: Any misstatement found in testing should be reported as fraud.
exam_traps.why: Without signs of intent it may be an honest mistake. Look for a pattern, concealment or resistance to correction first.

key_terms.definition: A deliberate act using deception, concealment or breach of trust to gain something the person or organization has no right to.
The deliberate purpose behind an act; the feature that separates fraud from error.
One piece of internal audit work with its own objectives and scope.

subtopics.name: The Fraud Triangle
subtopics.definition: The fraud triangle is a model of three conditions that accompany a fraud: motivation, opportunity and rationalization.
subtopics.why_it_matters: The triangle turns a vague worry into three questions for any process: who is under pressure, where could they act unseen, and how would they excuse it?
how_it_works: Motivation is the incentive or pressure to act: personal debt, a bonus tied to targets, or fear of missing a sales or profit goal.
Opportunity is a gap that lets the act happen and stay hidden: one person controlling a whole transaction, shared passwords, or unreviewed payments.
Rationalization is the excuse that makes the act feel acceptable: 'they treat me unfairly', 'the company can afford it'.
The syllabus says motivation, while the 2026 IIA and Anti-Fraud Collaboration white paper says incentive or pressure. It is the same side.
Controls act mainly on opportunity, the side a practitioner in that paper says internal auditors can most directly affect. Pressure and rationalization sit in people and culture.
One side alone proves nothing: hard targets are a reason to look closer at controls, not evidence of fraud.
subtopics.example: Internal auditor Tariq is planning a review of a regional sales office of a Jordanian telecom company. The quarterly bonus pays only above 110% of target (motivation), the sales manager can both create customer accounts and approve credits (opportunity), and staff say head office 'sets impossible numbers' (rationalization). Tariq adds account creation and credit approvals to the risks to test.

review: Evaluate incentive schemes for targets that invite manipulation
Identify roles where one person can act and conceal unseen
evidence: Incentive plan documents and target-setting papers
Staff survey or exit interview themes about pressure and fairness
audit_focus.recommend: Urge senior management to review targets and rewards that create undue pressure and to close the control gaps found.
audit_focus.decides: Senior management sets targets and rewards; the board oversees them

subtopics.isaca_rule: Know all three sides and which one controls reach. Segregation of duties, approvals and reviews reduce opportunity; pressure and rationalization are read from targets, rewards, culture and tone at the top.

exam_traps.trap: Strong process controls remove all three sides of the triangle.
exam_traps.why: Controls mostly close opportunity. A pressured person with an excuse may still collude or override, so culture and oversight matter too.

exam_traps.trap: A department under heavy target pressure must be committing fraud.
exam_traps.why: One side of the triangle is a risk indicator, not proof. It directs the auditor to the related controls.

key_terms.definition: The incentive or pressure that pushes a person toward fraud, such as debt or a target-based bonus.
A weakness that lets a person commit fraud and expect not to be caught.
The personal excuse a person uses to make a dishonest act feel justified.

subtopics.memory_aid: Why would they, how could they, and how would they excuse it?

subtopics.name: Recognizing Where Fraud Could Happen
subtopics.definition: A fraud risk is the possibility that someone will deliberately deceive in order to take assets, misstate information or gain an improper advantage in an activity.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Fraud risk is pervasive: it can sit in any process, at any level. An internal auditor who knows the usual conditions spots exposure early, before tests are designed around honest mistakes only.
how_it_works: Ask of each activity how someone could deliberately misstate, steal or conceal, and who would be motivated and able to do it.
Look for value that is easy to move: cash, payments, payroll, stock, refunds, and information such as customer data.
Look for open doors: one person handling a whole transaction, wide system access, shared passwords, or no independent review.
Look for pressure: bonuses tied to results, ambitious targets, or a culture where bad news is not tolerated.
Consider outsiders as well: suppliers, customers and cyber criminals, sometimes working with an insider.
A clean past does not lower the risk: fraud is hidden by design, so 'never had fraud here' is a belief, not evidence.
subtopics.example: During a walk-through at a fuel depot in Kenya, internal auditor Chebet learns that one clerk orders fuel, receives deliveries and adjusts the stock system, and that tank levels are checked against records once a year. Nobody has reported a loss. Chebet records theft of fuel hidden by system adjustments as a fraud risk in the engagement risk assessment.

review: Walk one transaction from start to finish and note who touches it
Compare system access rights with each person's assigned duties
Trace bonus and target rules to the figures staff can influence
evidence: System access listing matched to job roles
Process map showing who initiates, approves and records
Bonus plan and target documents for the unit
audit_focus.recommend: Ask the management of the activity to separate conflicting duties or add an independent review where one person controls a transaction.
audit_focus.decides: Management of the activity decides how to respond to each fraud risk

subtopics.isaca_rule: Fraud risk is a possibility, not a finding. Recognize it from conditions (value, access, pressure, weak review); do not wait for a past case or a tip. Must: consider it in every engagement risk assessment (Standard 13.2).

exam_traps.trap: No fraud has been found here before, so the fraud risk is low.
exam_traps.why: Fraud is concealed, so an absence of known cases says little. Exposure is judged from conditions and controls.

exam_traps.trap: Fraud risk matters only in finance and accounting processes.
exam_traps.why: Fraud can involve operations, procurement, data and nonfinancial reports. Any activity with value and opportunity is exposed.

key_terms.definition: The chance that deliberate deception will harm an objective of an activity or the organization.
A risk that can arise in many processes and units at once; the Standards give fraud as an example.
Fraud committed against the organization by outside parties, such as suppliers or customers.

subtopics.name: Common Fraud Schemes
subtopics.definition: A fraud scheme is the method used to commit and hide a fraud; schemes are commonly grouped into fraudulent reporting (financial or nonfinancial), asset misappropriation and corruption.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Naming the scheme tells the internal auditor which records to distrust and which control should have stopped it. A vague fear of fraud cannot be tested; a named scheme can.
how_it_works: Fraudulent reporting misstates information on purpose: sales invented or recorded early to meet a target, or uncollectible debts hidden with journal entries.
Asset misappropriation takes or misuses resources: inflated hours, payroll diverted to a private account, payment for goods never delivered, stock or customer data taken.
Corruption is misuse of position for an improper benefit, such as a bribe from a supplier, often alongside an undisclosed personal interest.
A scheme has two parts, the act and the cover. Forged signatures, altered documents and false entries are common cover.
Collusion lets a scheme pass controls that depend on people checking each other.
The four categories below follow the COSO and ACFE Fraud Risk Management Guide, which splits reporting into financial and nonfinancial.

types.meaning: Deliberate misstatement of financial results or disclosures.
Deliberate misstatement of other reported information, such as safety, quality or sustainability figures.
Theft or misuse of the organization's cash, goods, equipment or information.
Misuse of position for an improper benefit, such as taking a bribe.

subtopics.example: A grain cooperative in Argentina pays a transport contractor. Internal auditor Joaquín notes three facts: invoices for trips the weighbridge never recorded, approval by a logistics supervisor who is the contractor's cousin, and round amounts paid within a day. Joaquín classes the risk as asset misappropriation through false billing, with possible corruption, and plans tests matching invoices to weighbridge records.

review: Match a sample of supplier invoices to independent delivery records
Inspect manual journal entries posted near period end for support
Compare supplier and employee master data for shared details
evidence: Journal entry listing with preparer, approver and support
Conflict of interest declarations by staff who select suppliers
audit_focus.recommend: Advise management to map each family of fraud scheme to the control meant to stop or reveal it.
audit_focus.decides: Management decides which controls address each scheme

subtopics.isaca_rule: Classify a scheme by the act: reported information is falsified (fraudulent reporting), assets or data are taken or misused (asset misappropriation), or a position is misused for gain (corruption). The family points to the control that failed.

exam_traps.trap: Fraud always means stealing cash or goods.
exam_traps.why: Misstating results to earn a bonus or hide a loss is fraud too, even when nothing leaves a safe or warehouse.

exam_traps.trap: A bribe paid to win business is not fraud, because the organization benefits.
exam_traps.why: The Standards' definition covers an unjust or illegal business advantage as well as personal gain. Corruption is a fraud family.

key_terms.definition: The method by which a fraud is carried out and hidden.
Two or more people working together to get around a control.
Offering or taking something of value to influence a decision improperly.

topics.topic_name: Weighing fraud risk in an engagement
topics.overview: Every engagement risk assessment must consider fraud. This topic covers that requirement, how auditors think through fraud scenarios while planning, and how to judge which processes are exposed enough to change the engagement's objectives, scope, tests or team.
can_do: Decide when fraud risk must be considered in an engagement and what differs for advisory work
Judge from planning facts which fraud scenarios deserve testing
Determine which process in a scenario carries the greatest fraud exposure, and why
Decide what to adjust (objectives, scope, tests, skills) when fraud risk is significant

subtopics.name: Fraud in the Engagement Risk Assessment
subtopics.definition: The engagement risk assessment is the planning step in which internal auditors identify and rank the risks of the activity under review, fraud risks included.
subtopics.why_it_matters: This is where the Standards speak most directly about fraud. An engagement planned without asking how fraud could occur tests only for honest mistakes.
how_it_works: Standard 13.2 Engagement Risk Assessment requires internal auditors to consider fraud-related risks when identifying the risks to review, in every engagement and not only in fraud audits.
Standard 4.2 Due Professional Care adds that care includes weighing how probable significant errors, fraud and noncompliance are.
It happens in planning, before objectives, scope and the work program (the list of planned tests) are settled, so that fraud risks can shape them.
Fraud risks are ranked by likelihood and impact, and the most significant go into the work program.
In an advisory engagement (advice, with no assurance given), the agreement with stakeholders may make a formal, written risk assessment unnecessary.
If an earlier engagement assessed the same activity, the auditors review and update that assessment, fraud risks included.
subtopics.example: Engagement supervisor Ayasha reviews the planning file for an assurance engagement on grant payments at a Canadian arts council. The junior auditor left fraud out because the grants manager said the external auditors had found nothing. Ayasha returns the file: fraud risks such as false applicants and staff approving grants to relatives must be listed and rated before the work program is approved.

review: Inspect engagement planning files for documented fraud risks and their ratings
Trace each highly rated fraud risk to a planned test
evidence: Planning file pages listing fraud risks with likelihood and impact
Sign-off sheet showing who cleared the plan and when
audit_focus.recommend: Require the audit team to list and rate fraud risks in every planning file before testing begins.
audit_focus.decides: The chief audit executive or a delegated engagement supervisor approves the work program

subtopics.isaca_rule: Must: consider fraud risk in every engagement risk assessment, during planning. 'Only when management asks', 'only in a fraud audit' and 'after fieldwork' are wrong. May: for advisory work, the formal, documented assessment can be unnecessary.

exam_traps.trap: Fraud risk is assessed only in a fraud audit or when management asks.
exam_traps.why: Standard 13.2 makes it part of identifying risks in every engagement, whatever its label.

exam_traps.trap: An advisory engagement always needs a formal, documented fraud risk assessment.
exam_traps.why: For advisory work, the agreement with stakeholders decides whether a formal, documented assessment is needed.

key_terms.definition: Engagements where internal auditors test an activity against criteria and state a conclusion others can rely on.
Advice, started by internal auditors or on request, with no assurance given and no management responsibility taken on.

subtopics.name: Fraud Brainstorming and Scenario Thinking
subtopics.definition: Fraud brainstorming is a planning discussion in which the engagement team imagines how fraud could be committed and hidden in the activity.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Fraud is designed to pass ordinary checks. Thinking like someone who wants to beat the process shows which controls matter and where a routine sample would see nothing.
how_it_works: Gather information first: process documents, walk-throughs, interviews, earlier results, and risk assessments done by management or others.
Brainstorm scenarios: who could misstate, steal or conceal, with what access, under what pressure, and how it would be hidden.
Rate each fraud risk for significance, then decide which ones the engagement will examine further and with which tests.
Involve different levels and, where sensible, the business. Ask how a control could be done differently; owners rarely suspect their own area.

Treat management's fraud risk assessment as input: a Standard 9.4 consideration says to rely on management's risk information only after concluding its risk management processes are effective (a 'should').
Data analysis can show what interviews miss: outliers, overrides, policy exceptions and unseparated duties.
subtopics.example: Planning a procurement engagement at a Polish city transport operator, internal auditors Zofia and Emeka brainstorm with a buyer and a warehouse lead. Asked how the three-quote rule could be done differently, the buyer says quotes arrive by personal email. The team writes a scenario (one supplier sending all three quotes), rates it high, and adds a test of quote sources to the work program.

review: Inspect planning files for a record of the fraud scenario discussion
Confirm every top-ranked fraud idea led to a planned procedure
evidence: Session notes listing participants, scenarios and ratings
Software query results kept with the planning papers
audit_focus.recommend: Have the audit team hold and record a fraud scenario discussion while planning each assurance engagement.
audit_focus.decides: The chief audit executive or a delegate approves the resulting work program

subtopics.isaca_rule: Must: consider fraud risk during planning. Should: rely on management's assessment only after judging its process effective. Brainstorming itself is sound practice, not a Standards requirement.

exam_traps.trap: Management has already assessed fraud risk, so the auditor can adopt its ratings.
exam_traps.why: Management's view is input, to be relied on only once the risk management processes are judged effective.

exam_traps.trap: Brainstorming is best left until testing turns up something odd.
exam_traps.why: Its purpose is to shape objectives, scope and tests. After fieldwork it can no longer direct the work.

key_terms.definition: A team discussion during planning about how fraud could occur and be concealed in the activity.
Following one transaction from start to finish to see how the process really works.
Examining whole sets of records with software to find patterns, outliers and exceptions.

subtopics.name: Processes with High Fraud Exposure
subtopics.definition: Fraud exposure is how open a process is to fraud, judged from what is at stake, who has access, the pressure on people and the strength of controls.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Engagement time is limited. Judging exposure shows which processes need deeper tests, more experienced staff or specialist help.
how_it_works: The stakes are high when a process moves money or valuable assets, or produces figures that drive bonuses, funding or outside confidence.
Access is easy when a few people control the whole transaction, or system rights are wider than jobs need.
Pressure is strong where targets are demanding or rewards depend on one number; oversight is weak where reviews are routine and overrides are common.
Should: weigh fraud risks that span units (Standard 9.4 considerations); after a fraud, ask where its gap remains (position paper on fraud).

When exposure is significant, internal auditors propose changes to objectives and scope; the chief audit executive (CAE), or an engagement supervisor acting under delegation, must approve them (Standard 13.3).
Resource or skill gaps must be raised with the CAE (Standard 13.5 Engagement Resources).
subtopics.example: At a microfinance lender in Bangladesh, internal auditor Shirin compares two processes. Staff training has a small budget and three approvers. Loan disbursement moves cash daily, and branch officers both approve and release loans. Shirin rates disbursement as high exposure and proposes a wider scope and a data analysis specialist to the engagement supervisor, who approves under the CAE's delegation.

review: Compare each process step with who can initiate, approve, record and hold assets
Trace targets and ranking rules to the figures staff control
Sample overrides and policy exceptions for approval and stated reason
evidence: Data extract of overrides, exceptions and manual adjustments
User access report for the process systems
Target, ranking and incentive documents
audit_focus.recommend: Urge the management of the activity to strengthen review and separate duties in the steps that carry the highest fraud exposure.
audit_focus.decides: Management of the activity decides the control response and owns the risk

subtopics.isaca_rule: Exposure is a judgment from value, access, pressure and weak oversight, not department size or a clean record. Must: the CAE or a delegated engagement supervisor approves the scope changes internal auditors propose, and skill gaps are raised.

exam_traps.trap: The process with the largest budget always has the highest fraud risk.
exam_traps.why: Size is one factor. A smaller process with cash, one person in control and target pressure can be far more exposed.

exam_traps.trap: If the team lacks fraud-testing skills, the fraud risk can be left out of scope without comment.
exam_traps.why: Skill gaps go to the CAE, who can obtain the competencies. Silently dropping a significant risk hides a limit on the work.

key_terms.definition: The degree to which a process is open to fraud, given its value, access, pressure and controls.
What an engagement will and will not cover.

topics.topic_name: Fraud risk management and red flags
topics.overview: Organizations manage fraud risk through governance, risk assessment, controls, reporting channels, investigation and monitoring. This topic covers how an internal auditor evaluates that program, how to notice and weigh red flags across the organization and inside a process, and what to do with a red flag found during an engagement.
can_do: Judge whether an organization's fraud program has the parts a sound one needs
Weigh red flags in a scenario and decide whether they call for more work or escalation
Decide to whom, when and how a red flag found during an engagement is reported
Distinguish reporting an indicator from accusing a person or concluding that fraud occurred

subtopics.name: Evaluating Fraud Risk Management
subtopics.definition: Fraud risk management is the organization's set of policies, assessments, controls, reporting channels and responses for preventing, detecting and dealing with fraud.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Senior management is responsible for managing fraud risk and the board oversees it. The internal audit function gives assurance on whether the program is well designed and working, and advises on gaps.
how_it_works: Senior management designs and runs the program, the board oversees it, and internal audit assesses it.
The COSO and ACFE Fraud Risk Management Guide describes five parts: governance, risk assessment, preventive and detective controls, reporting and investigation, and monitoring.
For each part, the internal auditor asks whether it is adequately designed and operates effectively.
A sound fraud risk assessment names schemes, rates how likely and serious each is, maps existing controls, and acts on what remains.
The IIA's fraud position paper adds a response plan saying who does what when fraud is suspected and covering digital data, and calls qualified investigators essential.
Must: the internal audit plan considers fraud risk coverage (Standard 9.4).
subtopics.example: Internal auditor Babajide reviews fraud risk management at a Norwegian ferry operator. There is an anti-fraud policy and a hotline, but the last fraud risk assessment predates two new business lines, lists no schemes and has no owner, and nobody knows who would investigate a tip. Babajide reports the design as incomplete and recommends management assign an owner and update the assessment.

review: Compare the program with the five parts of a sound fraud risk program
Inspect the latest fraud risk assessment for schemes, ratings and owners
Trace two reported concerns from receipt to resolution
evidence: Case log showing intake, investigation and outcome dates
Latest fraud risk assessment document with its approval date
Board or committee minutes covering fraud reporting
audit_focus.recommend: Ask senior management to assign an owner, update the fraud risk assessment and define who investigates reported concerns.
audit_focus.decides: Senior management decides how to close gaps in the program

subtopics.isaca_rule: Management owns fraud risk management, the board oversees it, and internal audit evaluates and advises. Must: the internal audit plan considers coverage of fraud risk (Standard 9.4).

exam_traps.trap: Internal audit holds the main responsibility for preventing and detecting fraud.
exam_traps.why: Management does. Internal audit helps deter and detect fraud by assessing fraud risks and anti-fraud controls and advising, without taking on management's responsibility.

exam_traps.trap: An anti-fraud policy and a hotline show that fraud risk management is effective.
exam_traps.why: Those are two pieces of design. Effectiveness also needs a current risk assessment, working controls, a tested response and monitoring.

key_terms.definition: A structured review that identifies possible fraud schemes, rates them and maps the controls against them.
Written policies and investigation methods saying who does what when fraud is suspected, digital data included.
Discouraging fraud by making it likely that anyone who tries will be caught and punished.

subtopics.name: Red Flags Across the Organization and in a Process
subtopics.definition: A red flag is a fact, pattern or behavior suggesting that fraud may be present and deserves a closer look; it is an indicator, not proof.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Most frauds are hidden, so internal auditors meet them first as small oddities. Weighing them calmly avoids blindness and false accusation.
how_it_works: Organization-wide flags include heavy target pressure, leaders who set controls aside or discourage questions, a belief that fraud cannot happen here, and shared passwords.
Process flags include many corrections or reversals, reconciling items left open or undated, missing documents, results that are always good, and slow answers to audit requests.
Behavioral flags reported in fraud examiners' surveys include living beyond one's means, money troubles, closeness to a supplier, refusing to share duties and defensiveness.
Weigh a flag before acting: is there an innocent explanation, does independent evidence support it, is it a pattern, and what could be lost?
Must: seek more evidence when information looks incomplete, inconsistent or misleading (Standard 4.3); judge whether support that cannot be produced is itself a finding (Standard 14.1).
subtopics.example: Reviewing a supplier ledger reconciliation at a Chilean winery, internal auditor Renata sees six undated reconciling items carried for five months, and three requests for support went unanswered. Renata widens the sample and obtains bank records directly. They show a bank that posts credits late, and the accountant had been on leave. Renata reports the stale items as a control weakness, not as suspected fraud.

review: Compare the flagged item with independent records obtained directly
Sample similar transactions to see whether the oddity repeats
Trace who created, approved and changed the flagged entries
evidence: System audit trail of who posted and changed entries
Bank or third-party records obtained directly
Aged list of unresolved differences with supporting papers
audit_focus.recommend: Advise senior management to arrange an investigation by qualified people when indicators remain unexplained after follow-up.
audit_focus.decides: Senior management or the board, under the fraud response plan, decides whether to investigate

subtopics.isaca_rule: A red flag starts work; it does not end it. Must: seek more evidence (Standard 4.3). Corroborate with independent evidence, look for a pattern, and treat no single flag as proof.

exam_traps.trap: One red flag, such as an employee's expensive car, is enough to conclude that fraud occurred.
exam_traps.why: A single flag can have an innocent cause. It justifies more evidence and escalation of facts, never a conclusion about a person.

exam_traps.trap: A reasonable explanation from the manager closes the matter.
exam_traps.why: Skepticism means corroborating statements with independent evidence. If the person explaining could be involved, sound practice is to stop asking them and report (see 1D3.3).

key_terms.definition: An unbiased, questioning attitude: critically assessing whether information is reliable before relying on it.
A known difference between two records, waiting to clear, such as a payment not yet on the bank statement.

subtopics.name: Reporting Red Flags Found During an Engagement
subtopics.definition: Reporting a red flag means passing documented facts that may indicate fraud, promptly, to people with authority to act, through the set channels.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Handled badly, a red flag can alert a wrongdoer, destroy evidence, harm an innocent person or let losses continue.
how_it_works: Document the facts and communicate them the way the chief audit executive's methodology sets (a 'should' under Standard 1.2), which usually starts with the engagement supervisor.
Do not wait for the final communication: a Standard 13.1 consideration expects urgent issues to be raised during the engagement. For suspected fraud, the methodology sets the recipient.
The general route is in 1C3.3. Must: report under policy (Standard 1.2) and law (Standard 1.3). Should: senior management matters reach the board and are followed up.
Open questions suit an unexplained inconsistency (see 1B5.3). Once facts point to concealment, or to the person who would answer, stop asking and keep the matter from anyone involved.
Standard 1.1 Honesty and Professional Courage forbids hiding or leaving out findings.
subtopics.example: While testing travel claims at a Malaysian engineering firm, internal auditor Hafiz finds that the chief financial officer approved eleven of their own claims using altered hotel receipts. Hafiz secures copies and follows the function's methodology, which sends suspected fraud to the chief audit executive (CAE). Because a member of senior management is involved, the CAE reports to the board's audit committee.

review: Trace suspected fraud reports to the recipient the methodology names
Compare the date each indicator was found with the date it was reported
evidence: Written procedure naming who is told of a possible fraud
Log of indicators raised during engagements, with dates and recipients
audit_focus.recommend: Ask the chief audit executive to set out in the methodology who receives a suspected fraud report and how quickly.
audit_focus.decides: Senior management or the board decides whether to investigate

subtopics.isaca_rule: Must: report through the channel that policy and law set, and never hide a finding. Should: follow the CAE's methodology and confirm action on senior management matters reported to the board. Sound practice, not Standards lines: stop questioning anyone who may be involved, report indicators and leave confrontation to investigators.

exam_traps.trap: Discuss the red flag with the management of the activity first, like any other finding.
exam_traps.why: Policy and the CAE's methodology set the route. A manager who may be involved, or could alert the person involved, is not told first.

exam_traps.trap: Go straight to the police or a regulator.
exam_traps.why: Outside reporting follows what laws, regulations and policies specify. Acting alone may breach confidentiality and harm an investigation.

key_terms.definition: The chief audit executive's documented way of working, which internal auditors follow.
The communication issued at the end of an engagement with its results, often a written report.

topics.topic_name: Controls that prevent and detect fraud
topics.overview: Fraud controls either stop a fraud before it happens (preventive) or reveal it soon afterward (detective). This topic explains tone at the top, segregation of duties and authority levels, and the detective controls the syllabus names: reconciliations, supervisory reviews and whistleblower hotlines. No control gives absolute assurance, because collusion and management override can defeat it.
can_do: Explain how tone at the top raises or lowers the chance of fraud
Describe which duties are kept apart and what management can do when they cannot be
Explain how approval limits prevent fraud and how people get around them
Tell preventive from detective fraud controls in a short scenario

subtopics.name: Tone at the Top and the Likelihood of Fraud
subtopics.definition: Tone at the top is the message about integrity that the board and senior management send through what they say, do, reward and tolerate.
subtopics.why_it_matters: People copy what leaders reward. Leaders who bend rules hand staff a ready excuse and weaken every other control.
how_it_works: The board and senior management set the tone; senior management carries it into the culture, and the board oversees how management lives up to it.
Tone works on the human sides of the fraud triangle: it weakens rationalization and, through realistic targets and fair rewards, eases undue pressure.
It shows in actions more than documents: how leaders react to bad news, and whether rule-breakers who deliver results are disciplined.
The board is a check on management override and deals with allegations about senior management.
A code of conduct shows intent only; the tone is real when the code is followed at the top and enforced equally for everyone.
Internal auditors must encourage an ethics-based culture and report conduct that breaks the organization's ethical expectations (Standard 1.2 Organization's Ethical Expectations).
subtopics.example: A Ghanaian mobile money company has a clear code of conduct. Internal auditor Akosua learns that the top-selling regional head was caught backdating agent contracts and received only a private warning, then the annual sales award. Staff now describe backdating as tolerated. Akosua reports that the enforced tone contradicts the written one and raises fraud likelihood wherever staff saw it.

review: Compare disciplinary outcomes for senior and junior staff after similar breaches
Sample ethics survey and hotline data for themes about leaders
Trace incentive plans to the pressure they put on reported results
evidence: Disciplinary case records by grade and outcome
Staff ethics survey results and hotline statistics
Code of conduct sign-offs and training completion records
audit_focus.recommend: Urge senior management to apply the same consequences to everyone and review incentives that reward results at any cost.
audit_focus.decides: The board holds senior management to account for its conduct

subtopics.isaca_rule: A weak tone raises the likelihood of fraud even where process controls look strong. Judge tone by what leaders enforce (see 1C2.1 for culture and the control environment). Must: encourage an ethics-based culture.

exam_traps.trap: Tone at the top matters only for fraud by senior executives.
exam_traps.why: Tone shapes pressure and rationalization at every level: staff who see leaders bend rules, or face targets that cannot be met honestly, find fraud easier to excuse.

exam_traps.trap: Good process controls make tone at the top irrelevant to fraud.
exam_traps.why: Controls can be overridden by management or beaten by collusion. Culture decides whether people try, and whether others speak up.

key_terms.definition: The example about integrity and control set by the board and senior management.
A manager using their position to set a control aside.
Shared values and habits that make honest behavior the normal, expected choice.

subtopics.name: Segregation of Duties
subtopics.definition: Segregation of duties is the practice of dividing a transaction's key steps among different people so that no one person can both commit and hide a fraud.
subtopics.why_it_matters: It is the main control against opportunity. If one person can start, approve and record a transaction and hold the asset, nothing independent checks it.
how_it_works: The steps to keep apart are initiating a transaction, approving it, recording it, handling the money or goods, and reconciling the records.
It applies inside systems too: the person who creates a supplier should not be able to approve its payments.
It works before the event, which is why it counts as a preventive control.
Shared passwords, staff covering for each other, and one manager holding several system roles quietly cancel the separation.
Collusion defeats it: two people acting together can pass a control that depends on their independence.
Where full separation is not practical, as in a small team, management chooses compensating controls such as closer supervisory review.
subtopics.example: At the three-person finance office of a New Zealand honey exporter, internal auditor Hemi finds that the accountant sets up suppliers, enters invoices and releases bank payments. Hiring is impossible. Hemi recommends that management move payment release to the owner and have the owner review a monthly report of new suppliers and changed bank details.

review: Compare system access rights with a matrix of conflicting duties
Sample transactions and confirm different people initiated and approved them
Inspect how compensating controls operate where duties are combined
evidence: System-generated user access report with roles
Transaction logs showing initiator and approver identities
Records of supervisory review where duties are combined
audit_focus.recommend: Have the management of the activity remove conflicting access rights or add an independent review where duties cannot be separated.
audit_focus.decides: Management of the activity reduces or accepts any remaining conflict

subtopics.isaca_rule: No one person controls a transaction from start to finish. This is control practice, not a Standards requirement. Test whether the separation is real in system access; where it is not achievable, expect compensating controls chosen by management.

exam_traps.trap: Duties are separated on the organization chart, so the control is working.
exam_traps.why: Shared logins, wide system access or colleagues covering for each other can undo it. The test is who can actually do what.

exam_traps.trap: A small team that cannot separate duties has no acceptable control option.
exam_traps.why: Management can choose compensating controls, such as an owner's or supervisor's review of that person's work.

key_terms.definition: Dividing a transaction's key steps among different people so that no one can make and hide an error or fraud alone.
Tasks that, held by one person, would let that person both make and hide an error or fraud.
A common-usage term for an alternative control that reduces risk when the preferred control is not practical.

subtopics.name: Authority Levels and Approval Limits
subtopics.definition: Authority levels are documented limits on who may approve which transactions and up to what amount, with larger or riskier items needing a more senior approver.
subtopics.why_it_matters: An approval limit puts a second, accountable person before a transaction, shrinking one person's opportunity to commit the organization improperly.
how_it_works: A delegation of authority sets limits by role: a supervisor approves up to one amount, a director up to more, the board above that.
The control is preventive: the transaction should not go ahead until someone with enough authority, independent of the requester, has approved it.
Limits are strongest when the system enforces them. Where nothing stops or catches a release made without approval, the limit is weak in design.
People get around a limit by splitting one purchase into several smaller ones, approving their own request, or having a senior manager override the rule.
An approver who signs without reading the support adds no control: approving means checking that the transaction is valid, supported and within policy.
subtopics.example: A Dubai hotel group requires a director's approval for purchases above 20,000 dirhams. Internal auditor Samira analyzes purchase data and finds 14 orders to one decorator, each between 19,500 and 19,900 dirhams, all approved by one purchasing supervisor. Samira documents the pattern as possible splitting, extends the analysis to every supplier, and reports it as a fraud indicator.

review: Compare approvals in a transaction sample with the delegation of authority
Sample purchases just below limits by supplier and period
Reperform an approval attempt beyond a test user's limit
evidence: Data analysis of transactions clustered just under approval thresholds
Screenshot of the thresholds configured for each role
Current delegation of authority with its approval record
audit_focus.recommend: Ask management to make the system apply approval limits to the whole purchase, not each order, and monitor clusters just below them.
audit_focus.decides: Senior management, within powers the board has set, decides who may approve what

subtopics.isaca_rule: Approval limits prevent fraud only when the approver is independent, has the authority and truly reviews, and nothing lets a transaction skip the approval unseen. Authority levels may prevent fraud. Clusters just under a limit are a common warning sign in practice, not a Standards rule.

exam_traps.trap: Authority limits are detective controls because they involve a review.
exam_traps.why: The approval comes before the transaction goes ahead, so it prevents. A check after the event, such as a reconciliation, detects.

exam_traps.trap: Every transaction was approved, so the authority control is effective.
exam_traps.why: Approvals by the requester, above the approver's limit, or of split purchases defeat it. Test who approved, when, and for how much.

key_terms.definition: The largest amount or the type of transaction that a role may approve.
Breaking one transaction into smaller ones so that each falls below an approval limit.
A control that acts before an event to stop it from happening.

subtopics.name: Detective Controls: Reconciliations, Supervisory Review and Hotlines
subtopics.definition: Detective fraud controls are checks that reveal a fraud or error after it has occurred, soon enough to limit the loss and trace what happened.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Prevention never works perfectly, because people collude and managers override. Detective controls shorten the time a fraud runs, and known checks discourage people from trying.
how_it_works: A reconciliation compares two records that should agree, such as the ledger and the bank statement, and follows up every difference.
A supervisory review is a manager's examination of work, exceptions and reports for items that are unusual or unsupported.

A whistleblower hotline takes confidential, often anonymous, reports from employees and others. The COSO and ACFE Fraud Risk Management Guide cites research ranking tips first among ways frauds are found.
Each works only when done by someone independent of the work checked, on time, with differences and reports followed up.
The syllabus lists all three as controls that detect fraud; the same guide also credits reporting systems with preventing and deterring it.
The Standards name four control types in a consideration to Standard 13.2: preventive, detective, directive and corrective (see 1C7.2).

rows.label: What it does
cells: Matches two records and explains each difference
A manager examines work, exceptions and reports

rows.label: What it can reveal
cells: Missing cash, false entries, unrecorded items
Schemes hidden from the records, collusion, override

rows.label: What weakens it
cells: Prepared by the person who keeps the records; old items left open
Signing without reading; no follow-up of exceptions
Fear of retaliation; reports not investigated

subtopics.example: At a university bookshop in Trinidad, the cashier also prepares the daily till-to-bank reconciliation, and it always balances. An anonymous hotline call says refunds are being faked. Internal auditor Dwayne notes that the reconciler was not independent, passes the tip to the chief audit executive, and recommends that management assign the reconciliation to someone outside the bookshop.

review: Reperform a sample of reconciliations and trace old open items
Inspect review evidence for questions raised, not only signatures
Trace hotline reports from intake to documented outcome
evidence: Reperformed reconciliations compared with the originals
Hotline case log with dates, handling and outcomes
Review sign-offs with notes on exceptions followed up
audit_focus.recommend: Advise management to assign reconciliations and reviews to staff independent of the work and track open items to closure.
audit_focus.decides: Management owns the detective controls; the board oversees how reported concerns are handled

subtopics.isaca_rule: Reconciliations, supervisory reviews and hotlines detect; segregation of duties and approval limits prevent. The grouping comes from the syllabus, not a Standards requirement. A detective control done by the person whose work it checks, or never followed up, is not operating.

exam_traps.trap: A hotline with no calls shows there is no fraud.
exam_traps.why: Silence can mean fear of retaliation or doubt that reports are acted on. A hotline detects only when people trust it.

exam_traps.trap: The reconciliation is signed off, so it is effective.
exam_traps.why: A sign-off over old unexplained items, or one prepared by the person who records the transactions, gives little assurance.

key_terms.definition: A control that acts after an event to reveal that it happened.
Information about suspected wrongdoing passed on by an employee, supplier or customer.
Punishing a person for raising a concern in good faith.

topics.overview: Investigating fraud is specialist work. This topic covers the internal audit function's role, which depends on its mandate and its competencies, and then, at recognition level, how interviews, investigations and fraud tests are approached. It ends with how internal auditors work with fraud investigators and use what they know.
can_do: Explain what decides whether internal audit investigates a suspected fraud
Recognize sound and unsound interviewing practice in a short scenario
Recognize common investigation steps and fraud tests, and what each is for
Identify the information held by investigators that helps plan audit work

subtopics.name: The Internal Audit Function's Role in Investigations
subtopics.definition: The internal audit function's investigation role is whatever its mandate assigns and its competencies allow; investigating is not automatically part of internal auditing.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Investigations can end in dismissal, recovery action or prosecution. Without authority or skill, the work can spoil evidence and accuse the wrong person.
how_it_works: The mandate comes first: the charter may name the function's services, and the Standards give investigations as an example (a consideration to Standard 6.1 Internal Audit Mandate).
Competency comes second: internal auditors must take on only services they have, or can obtain, the competencies for (Standard 3.1 Competency).
The chief audit executive (CAE) must make sure the function as a whole has the competencies its charter needs, or obtains them.
The IIA's position paper on fraud says investigating is not normally internal audit's job and is best done by people experienced in it.

Every internal auditor should still know enough about fraud to spot red flags, judge whether to recommend an investigation, and evaluate anti-fraud controls (position paper; a Standard 3.1 consideration).
After a fraud, internal audit's part is to learn how the controls failed and recommend improvements.
subtopics.example: A hotline report alleges theft of ticket revenue at a Peruvian rail operator, and the chief executive officer asks CAE Rosa to investigate. The charter lists investigations, but nobody on the team has the experience. Rosa tells the chief executive officer and the audit committee chair, proposing that an outside forensic firm lead and internal audit supply process knowledge.

review: Compare the charter's list of services with investigations actually performed
Inspect the fraud response plan for who leads each type of case
Evaluate investigators' qualifications against the cases assigned to them
evidence: Board-approved internal audit charter naming the services
Fraud response plan with roles and escalation routes
Skills records or contracts for the investigators used
audit_focus.recommend: Have senior management and the board define in the fraud response plan who investigates and when specialists are engaged.
audit_focus.decides: The board approves the charter that sets internal audit's investigation role

subtopics.isaca_rule: Two tests: is it in the mandate, and are the competencies there? Must: have or obtain the competencies. Should: every internal auditor knows fraud red flags. Internal audit does not lead an investigation by default.

exam_traps.trap: Internal audit leads every fraud investigation because it is independent.
exam_traps.why: Independence is not investigative skill or authority. The role comes from the mandate and needs experienced people.

exam_traps.trap: Internal auditors need no fraud knowledge when a separate investigations unit exists.
exam_traps.why: They must still consider fraud risk in every engagement (Standard 13.2), and should know enough to recognize red flags and evaluate anti-fraud controls.

key_terms.definition: Specialist fact-finding on records and data; the Standards list it as an example of advisory services.
The board-approved document holding the function's mandate, position and reporting lines.

subtopics.name: Interviewing Techniques
subtopics.definition: Interviewing is gathering information by asking people planned questions; in fraud-related work its aim is facts, never an accusation.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Interviews show how a process really runs and what people have seen. Handled badly, they warn a wrongdoer, pressure an innocent person or produce statements nobody can rely on.
how_it_works: Prepare first: learn the process, read the documents, decide which facts are needed, and plan whom to see and what to ask.
Start with open questions that invite explanation ('Walk me through how a refund is approved'), then narrow to dates, amounts and names.
Ask how a control could be done differently or bypassed; people describe weaknesses more freely than fraud.
Stay neutral and respectful: Standard 1.1 requires truthful, respectful communication even when expressing skepticism. No threats, tricks or accusations.
Treat answers as information to corroborate against documents, data or an independent person, not as proof.
Record who attended and what was said. Questioning a suspected person is left to trained investigators.
subtopics.example: Petty cash keeps running short at a Samoan resort. Keen to help, internal auditor Sina asks the night clerk outright whether the supervisor is stealing. The clerk warns the supervisor, and two count sheets vanish before the investigators arrive. Sina's next interview is different: an open request to describe the end-of-shift count, careful listening, and notes written up the same day.

review: Inspect interview records for attendees, date and what was said
Compare interview statements with documents or data that corroborate them
evidence: Interview plans listing the facts sought and the people seen
Dated interview notes kept in the workpapers
audit_focus.recommend: Train internal audit staff in fact-finding interviews and refer suspect interviews to trained investigators.
audit_focus.decides: Management or the board, under the fraud response plan, assigns investigators

subtopics.isaca_rule: Must: communicate truthfully and respectfully (Standard 1.1) and seek evidence for what is said (Standard 4.3). The questioning technique itself is general practice, not a Standards line. Accusing or confronting a suspect is left to trained investigators.

exam_traps.trap: A good fraud interview confronts the person early to get a confession.
exam_traps.why: Confrontation by an untrained auditor risks a wrongful accusation and damaged evidence. Suspect interviews belong to trained investigators.

exam_traps.trap: What a credible manager says in an interview can be taken as fact.
exam_traps.why: Skepticism requires corroboration. A statement is weaker than evidence the auditor obtains directly or from an independent source.

key_terms.definition: A question that asks for an explanation in the person's own words, not a yes or no.
A question answered with a specific fact, such as yes, no, a date or an amount.
A question worded so that it suggests the answer the interviewer wants.

subtopics.name: Investigation and Fraud Testing Techniques
subtopics.definition: Investigation techniques establish the facts of a suspected fraud; fraud tests are audit procedures that look for signs of deliberate manipulation in records.
subtopics.why_it_matters: At this level the task is recognition: what these methods are, what each is for, and why evidence must stay usable later.
how_it_works: A sound investigation is prompt, competent and confidential, and follows a process planned in advance.
The typical steps are to secure the evidence, examine documents and data, interview people, analyze the facts, report to those with authority, and fix the root cause.
Evidence, including digital evidence, must be collected lawfully and kept intact, respecting access rights and legal requirements.
Specialists join as needed: legal counsel, human resources, fraud examiners, digital forensic experts or outside investigators.
Fraud tests use data analysis over whole populations to find trends, outliers, manual overrides and unreported policy exceptions.
Other tests include tracing transactions to source documents, confirming facts with independent third parties, comparing related figures such as payroll cost and headcount, and widening a sample.
subtopics.example: After a tip about fake suppliers at a Hungarian printing company, the audit committee appoints an outside forensic firm. Internal auditor Bence supports it by comparing every supplier's bank account and address with the employee master file. Three match. Bence does not question the employees, keeps the data extract unchanged with a note of how it was obtained, and hands over the results.

review: Sample closed cases and compare their handling with the fraud response plan
Inspect how evidence was secured and who had access to it
Evaluate whether root causes of confirmed cases were fixed
evidence: Case files with dated evidence logs and approvals
Records of legal advice on evidence collection
Corrective action tracking for confirmed cases
audit_focus.recommend: Ask management to document investigation procedures, including evidence handling and when legal counsel and specialists are engaged.
audit_focus.decides: Senior management, advised by legal counsel, decides on discipline, recovery and referral

subtopics.isaca_rule: Recognize each method and its purpose. Must: stay within your competence (Standard 3.1). Evidence is secured lawfully and kept intact, people with investigation skills lead, and data analysis over the full population is a typical fraud test.

exam_traps.trap: The auditor should copy the suspect's mailbox and files at once so no evidence is lost.
exam_traps.why: Collecting digital evidence without proper authority and method can break the law and make the evidence unusable.

exam_traps.trap: Fraud testing just means a larger random sample of the same documents.
exam_traps.why: Forged documents can pass a sample check. Fraud tests look for patterns across all the data and confirm facts independently.

key_terms.definition: Specialist collection and examination of electronic evidence so it stays reliable and lawful to use.
Keeping evidence unchanged and traceable from the moment it is obtained.
Asking an independent third party to verify a fact, such as a balance.

subtopics.name: Working with Fraud Investigators
subtopics.definition: Coordination with fraud investigators is the sharing of plans, results and risk information between the internal audit function and those who investigate fraud, within confidentiality rules.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Investigators hold some of the best fraud risk information in the organization. Ignoring it leaves the audit blind to schemes already tried.
how_it_works: They hold useful information: their fraud risk assessments, past investigation files, trends across cases, and whistleblower complaints.
In planning, the internal auditor may review recent risk assessments made by others and meet other assurance and advisory providers (Standard 13.2 considerations).
Trends point to exposure: several cases of one scheme, or complaints clustered on one unit, show where to test and feed the internal audit plan.
The chief audit executive (CAE) is required to coordinate with other assurance providers and to consider relying on their work (Standard 9.5 Coordination and Reliance).
Confidentiality binds both sides: case details and whistleblower identities are shared only as policy and law allow (Standard 5.2 Protection of Information).
Avoid disturbing an open case: coordinate any audit testing that touches it with the investigators first (sound practice, not a Standards line).
subtopics.example: Before an engagement on claims handling at a South African insurer, internal auditor Sipho meets the investigations unit lead. The unit's summary shows nine cases of claims paid to bank accounts changed days before payment, and five hotline complaints about one branch. Sipho adds bank-detail changes to the engagement risk assessment, proposes bringing that branch into scope, and agrees how case data will be handled.

review: Compare investigation trends with the fraud risks in the engagement risk assessment
Sample closed cases and trace whether the control fixes were made
Inspect how hotline complaints are logged, assigned and resolved
evidence: Investigation case statistics by scheme, unit and year
Hotline complaint log with handling status
Notes of coordination meetings between internal audit and investigators
audit_focus.recommend: Advise management to share investigation trends and case outcomes with process owners and track the resulting control fixes.
audit_focus.decides: Management decides on control fixes; access to open case files follows policy and law

subtopics.isaca_rule: Must: the CAE coordinates with other assurance providers. May: review others' risk assessments when planning. The internal auditor uses investigators' risk assessments, past cases, trends and complaints as planning input and protects confidential details.

exam_traps.trap: Past investigation files are irrelevant once the cases are closed.
exam_traps.why: Closed cases show which schemes worked and which controls failed: direct evidence of exposure for the engagement risk assessment.

exam_traps.trap: Internal audit's access rights mean whistleblower identities can be shared freely within the team.
exam_traps.why: Access is for professional purposes only. Sensitive details go only to those who need them and are protected as policy and law require.

key_terms.definition: A pattern across cases, such as a repeated scheme, location or control weakness.
A concern about possible wrongdoing raised through a reporting channel, often in confidence.

key_terminologies.Fraud: A deliberate act using deception, concealment or breach of trust to gain something the person or organization has no right to.
key_terminologies.Fraud triangle: A model of three conditions that accompany fraud: motivation (incentive or pressure), opportunity (a gap in control) and rationalization (the excuse).
key_terminologies.Fraud risk: The chance that deliberate deception will harm an objective of an activity or the organization.
key_terminologies.Fraudulent reporting: Deliberate misstatement of financial or nonfinancial information.
key_terminologies.Asset misappropriation: Theft or misuse of the organization's cash, goods, equipment or information.
key_terminologies.Corruption: Misuse of position for an improper benefit, such as taking a bribe.
key_terminologies.Collusion: Two or more people working together to get around a control.
key_terminologies.Management override: A manager using their position to set a control aside.
key_terminologies.Red flag: A warning sign that fraud may exist; a reason to look closer, not proof.
key_terminologies.Professional skepticism: An unbiased, questioning attitude: critically assessing whether information is reliable before relying on it.
key_terminologies.Engagement: One piece of internal audit work with its own objectives and scope.
key_terminologies.Assurance services: Engagements where internal auditors test an activity against criteria and state a conclusion others can rely on.
key_terminologies.Advisory services: Advice, started by internal auditors or on request, with no assurance given and no management responsibility taken on.
key_terminologies.Chief audit executive (CAE): The head of the internal audit function, whatever the job title.
key_terminologies.Consideration for Implementation: A 'should' or 'may' in a standard: preferred or optional practice, not mandatory.
key_terminologies.Fraud risk management: The policies, assessments, controls and responses an organization uses to prevent, detect and deal with fraud.
key_terminologies.Fraud response plan: Written policies and investigation methods saying who does what when fraud is suspected, digital data included.
key_terminologies.Tone at the top: The example about integrity and control set by the board and senior management.
key_terminologies.Segregation of duties: Dividing a transaction's key steps among different people so that no one can make and hide an error or fraud alone.
key_terminologies.Authority level: The largest amount or the type of transaction that a role may approve.
key_terminologies.Preventive control: A control that acts before an event to stop it from happening.
key_terminologies.Detective control: A control that acts after an event to reveal that it happened.
key_terminologies.Reconciliation: Comparing two records that should agree and following up every difference.
key_terminologies.Supervisory review: A manager's examination of work, exceptions and reports for unusual or unsupported items.
key_terminologies.Whistleblower hotline: A confidential channel for reporting suspected wrongdoing, often anonymously.
key_terminologies.Fraud investigation: A structured inquiry by qualified people to establish the facts of a suspected fraud.
key_terminologies.Forensic services: Specialist fact-finding on records and data; the Standards list it as an example of advisory services.
key_terminologies.COSO: The Committee of Sponsoring Organizations (COSO) of the Treadway Commission, backed by five professional bodies including The IIA; it publishes control, risk and fraud guidance.
key_terminologies.ACFE: The Association of Certified Fraud Examiners, a professional body for anti-fraud specialists.
